newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK opens way for wholesale pension reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK opens way for wholesale pension reform.

text.p: Britain heralded the start of the biggest shake-up in its pension provision since World War Two with the launch on Thursday of a wide-ranging pensions review.
Central to the review will be the government's belief that the way ahead lies in people having access to a second pension to supplement the basic state pension.

Secretary of State for Social Security Harriet Harman said the government would be consulting widely on its proposals for 'stakeholder pensions' which the Labour Party pledged itself to in its election manifesto.
These will be provided by an alliance of employer and employee organisations and financial services companies and offer "secure, flexible and value-for-money" pensions.
The intention is to meet the needs of those unable to join an employer's occupational scheme, on modest incomes or those in intermittent employment such as women.
They could also provide a vehicle for smaller firms to make pension provision for their employees.
In addition, the government is proposing 'citizenship pensions' aimed at those, for example, caring for elderly relatives and unable to contribute to pensions in their own right.
Harman said both proposals would be implemented in the current session of Parliament which is expected to last until 2001 or early 2002.
The government promised that pensioners' organisations, employers, employees, consumers pensions experts would all have a chance to participate fully in the review.

The National Pensioners' Convention, chaired by former head of the Trade Union Congress Jack Jones and which represents over 1.5 million people, is to have a "specific and central" role in the review.
"Only by achieving a sustainable consensus for change can the country meet the pensions challenge" said Harman.
The Association of British insurers welcomed the announcement and Adrian Boulding, Legal & General's Pensions strategy director said the key themes would be simplicity and accessibility.
"I think we'll see stakeholder pensions providing a core basic level of pension provision... It may well resemble a Personal Equity Plan (PEP) with some contribution limit," said Boulding.
The initial framework for change following the review will be published in the first half of 1998.
But the government said it would stand by its manifesto commitment to retain the basic state pension and the state earnings related pension scheme (Serps).
The review is an attempt to head off the problems caused by an ageing population.
The basic state pension is expected to cost 31.9 billion pounds ($53.5 billion) this year, roughly one third of the country's total social security budget.
Another task for the review will be to establish the balance between public and private sectors.
This is likely to involve deciding what the government's role will be in approving providers of the new pensions.

The requirement of value for money, security and flexibility is likely to mean companies only being allowed to sell these pensions if they meet criteria such as on financial strength, charges, investment and service performance.

The government has hinted in the past that companies failing to meet the Government's December 1998 deadline for the settling compensation claims arising from the pensions mis-selling scandal of the late 1980s and 1990s could be excluded from provision of new second pensions.

The crisis in pension provision in Britain was highlighted by a damning OFT report on the shortcomings of existing pension products published earlier this week which called for radical changes to safeguard consumer interests.
Harman said the government wanted to support and strengthen the existing framework of occupational pension provision.
This might involve establishing a bechmark against which employers, employees and trustees could measure their own scheme, she said.
